abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a powerful tool for the design of flame-retardant polymeric materials, yet its progress remains constrained by the quality, comparability, and mechanistic relevance of available reaction-to-fire data. Flame retardancy is not a static material attribute; it is an emergent outcome of coupled heating, pyrolysis, ignition, gas-phase combustion, heat feedback, and condensed-phase reconstruction. Current data-driven studies still rely mainly on chemical descriptors, formulation information, and a limited set of outcome-based flammability metrics. Process-level information such as heat release, gas-phase product evolution, and condensed-phase structural change remains underused. In addition, the absence of a unified framework for data hierarchy, experimental conditions, and parameter definitions further limits model interpretability, transferability, and generalizability. This review establishes reaction-to-fire characterization as the experimental and data foundation for AI-assisted research on flame-retardant polymeric materials. We systematically examine fire-testing methods, parameter systems, and measurement conditions in relation to AI modeling, and propose a framework comprising five functional modules: fire-environment simulation, physical-parameter acquisition, gas-phase product diagnostics, condensed-phase product analysis, and interface configuration. Together, these modules link the coupled processes of polymer pyrolysis, gas-phase combustion, and condensed-phase evolution to structured, measurable data outputs. We further discuss how different types of reaction-to-fire data support structure-property analysis in flame-retardant polymeric materials, summarize current AI strategies and recent progress, and outline how mechanism-informed models can be built on more structured reaction-to-fire data. On this basis, we propose that the usefulness of reaction-to-fire data for AI depends not only on parameter availability, but also on whether the fire environment, measurement hierarchy, and process relevance are explicitly defined. Future AI studies on flame-retardant polymeric materials should therefore move beyond static structure-property fitting toward condition-explicit, process-constrained modeling rooted in reaction-to-fire characterization. This shift is expected to improve model interpretability, transferability, and design reliability.
